pll1d3c1-d1e3476.summary: Takes Rom 1:20 as the warrant for natural knowledge of God: 'creature of the world' means man, who by rational nature and through God's works, in which the craftsman's judgment shines, could and did perceive God's invisible things.
claims: Man could know God's invisible things through created works.
Rational nature and God's works enable knowledge of God.
God 'revealed' himself by making works that reflect the maker.

pll1d3c1-d1e3519.summary: First way, via Ambrose: God made a visible work so that the invisible maker might be known by the certain. Since no creature could make or destroy heaven and earth, their maker must be above every creature and so is God.
claims: The certain visible work leads to knowledge of the uncertain invisible maker.
What no creature can make reveals a maker above all creatures, who is God.

pll1d3c1-d1e3536.summary: Announces another rational way by which God's truth could be known.

pll1d3c1-d1e3540.summary: Gives Augustine's account of the Platonists' ascent: no body is God; nothing changeable is the supreme principle; so they transcended souls and changeable spirits, seeing that every changeable thing comes from one who is unchangeably and simply, maker of all and made by none.
claims: No body is God.
Nothing changeable is the supreme God.
Every changeable thing comes from an unchangeable and simple being.
God made all and was made by none.

pll1d3c1-d1e3562.summary: Continues the philosophers' reasoning: every substance is body or spirit, spirit is better than body, and the maker of both is far better.
claims: Spirit is better than body.
The maker of spirit and body is far better than both.

pll1d3c1-d1e3574.summary: Adds the argument from form: intelligible form ranks above sensible form, and since bodies and minds have form in greater or lesser degree, there must be a first, unchangeable, incomparable form by which they are formed, the unmade principle of all.
claims: Intelligible form is superior to sensible form.
Graded beauty implies a first and unchangeable form.
The principle of things is unmade and makes all.

pll1d3c1-d1e3583.summary: Explains why Paul says 'invisible things' in the plural although God is one simple essence without parts or accidents: God is known in many ways from creatures, as eternal, omnipotent, wise, and good, and all these point to the unity of the Godhead.
claims: God is a simple essence without diversity of parts or accidents.
The plural 'invisibilia' reflects many modes of knowing the one God.
From creatures God is known as eternal, omnipotent, wise, and good.

pll1d3c1-d1e3598.summary: Raises the next question: whether any trace of the Trinity, however slight, could be had from created things.

pll1d3c1-d1e3604.summary: Answers with De Trinitate VI: created things show unity, form (species), and order, in bodies and souls alike, so a vestige of the Trinity shines in creatures. In the Trinity are the supreme origin, most perfect beauty, and most blessed delight.
claims: A vestige of the Trinity appears in creatures.
Every creature has unity, species, and order.
In the Trinity are supreme origin, perfect beauty, and blessed delight.

pll1d3c1-d1e3623.summary: With De vera religione, assigns the triad to the persons: the Father as supreme origin, the Son as perfect beauty and form of all things, the Spirit as the goodness and gift that keeps creatures from perishing. From creatures we understand the Trinity of one substance: principle, form, and grace; author, likeness, and peace.
claims: The Father is the supreme origin.
The Son is the perfect beauty and form of all things.
The Holy Spirit is the goodness and gift of Father and Son.
From creatures we understand a Trinity of one substance.

pll1d3c1-d1e3654.summary: Sets the limit: creatures give some indication of the Trinity, but not sufficient knowledge without revelation through teaching or inward inspiration. The ancient philosophers saw the truth as in shadow and from afar and failed at the Trinity, like Pharaoh's magicians at the third sign. Creatures still help faith in invisible things.
claims: Contemplating creatures gives no sufficient knowledge of the Trinity without revelation.
The philosophers saw the truth only dimly and failed regarding the Trinity.
Creatures help faith in invisible things.

pl-l1d3c1.summary: Considers what can be known of God from creatures (Rom 1:20). Through rational nature and created works, humans, and especially the philosophers per Augustine's De civitate Dei VIII, could know that God is beyond every body, every changeable spirit, and every form, the unmade principle of all. The plural 'invisible things' is explained by the many ways the one simple God is known: eternal from perpetuity, omnipotent from magnitude, wise from order, good from governance. Creatures also bear a vestige of the Trinity in their unity, species, and order (Augustine), corresponding to Father as origin, Son as beauty, and Spirit as goodness or delight. Yet creatures cannot give sufficient knowledge of the Trinity without revelation; the philosophers saw it only as in shadow.
claims: God's existence and attributes can be known by reason from created things.
The philosophers ascended beyond bodies and changeable spirits to the unchangeable principle of all.
God is known as eternal, omnipotent, wise, and good from perpetuity, magnitude, order, and governance of creatures.
Creatures bear a vestige of the Trinity in their unity, species, and order.
Sufficient knowledge of the Trinity cannot be had from creatures without revelation.
